title: U.S. House · Kentucky's 1st District
area: Western Kentucky, including Paducah, Bowling Green's western suburbs, and the Jackson Purchase and Pennyrile regions.

candidates.name: James Comer
candidates.ballotNote: Won the May 19, 2026 Republican primary with 88.1% of the vote, defeating David Sims, Robert James Sutherby and Penny Arcos.
candidates.currentRole: U.S. Representative, Kentucky's 1st District (since 2016); Chair, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

summary.text: James Comer is the Republican incumbent for Kentucky's 1st Congressional District, first elected in 2016 and in office since November 2016. A Monroe County farmer and agribusiness owner, he served in the Kentucky House of Representatives and as Kentucky Commissioner of Agriculture before Congress. He chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and is also on the Education and Workforce Committee.

background.text: Born in Carthage, Tennessee, in 1972; according to his official biography he was raised in Monroe County, Kentucky.
Earned a bachelor's degree in agriculture from Western Kentucky University in 1993.

Business career includes co-owning the Comer Land and Cattle Company since 1994, serving as president of Comer and Polston Insurance Incorporated (1993-1995) and CFB Foods Incorporated (2001-2003), and as a director of South Central Bank (2000-2012).
Chaired the Monroe County Republican Party.
Served in the Kentucky House of Representatives, District 53, from 2001 to 2012.
Served as Kentucky Commissioner of Agriculture from 2012 to 2016; his official biography says he championed Kentucky's industrial hemp industry in that role.
Sought the 2015 Republican nomination for governor, losing the May 19 primary to Matt Bevin by 83 votes.
Took office in the U.S. House on November 14, 2016, succeeding Ed Whitfield; renominated in the May 19, 2026 Republican primary.
Chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and also serves on the Education and Workforce Committee.

priorities.text: Government Oversight and Reform: says the Oversight Committee under his leadership has investigated waste, fraud, abuse and mismanagement across the federal government, including pandemic relief fraud and improper payments.
Healthcare: says he supports protecting rural healthcare providers, strengthening Medicare, and giving patients greater control over their healthcare decisions.
Second Amendment: says he is a "strong defender of the Second Amendment" who opposes federal efforts to restrict the constitutional rights of law-abiding gun owners.

positions.summary: Says he opposes federal efforts to restrict gun rights, has voted against legislation criminalizing private firearm transfers and creating a national gun registry, and supports concealed-carry reciprocity.
positions.quote: Congressman Comer is a strong defender of the Second Amendment and opposes all efforts by the federal government to restrict the constitutional rights of law-abiding citizens. He has voted against legislation that would criminalize private firearm transfers, create unnecessary delays for lawful purchases, and move the country closer to a national gun registry.

record.text: Chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (119th Congress, 2025-2026) and also serves on the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
Chaired the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform in the 118th Congress (2023-2024) as well.

candidates.name: Drew Williams
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Democratic primary after the primary was canceled with no other candidates on the ballot.

summary.text: John "Drew" Williams is a lifelong resident of Marshall County, Kentucky, and a Murray State University history graduate who has worked in the family dock-building trade. Running as the Democratic nominee, he says he wants to bring more public engagement, such as town halls and issue-driven debates, into how he would represent the district.

background.text: Describes himself as a lifelong resident of Marshall County, Kentucky.
Graduated from Murray State University in 2016 with a degree in History and a minor in Biology.
Says he has spent nearly two decades working in family-owned businesses building docks and marinas across five states.
Says that since 2019 he and his wife have worked with the community to revitalize the Tater Day festival and that he has volunteered locally.

priorities.text: "I want to formalize our public townhalls, issue-driven debates, courthouse surveys, and expert roundtables to get a true understanding and perspective of where our community stands. It is my duty to vote based on that collectively gathered soft-data while working to be an advocate for the poor, marginalized, and disenfranchised."

researchNotes: Comer's federal key floor votes and FEC finance totals are added separately by script. His official issues pages (agriculture, education, healthcare, military, small business, transportation) largely describe general priorities rather than taking a stance on one of this guide's fixed issue statements; only his Second Amendment page directly addresses one. No specific issue positions with direct quotes were found for Williams beyond his general priorities statement (from his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, reproduced on the district election page). Williams's biography rests on his own Ballotpedia Candidate Connection statement; no campaign website was found.
